name: Mystery in Nature: Recognition Memory for Trail Scenes
description: Faithful replication of the recognition memory task (RMT) with the original images: 80 nature-trail photographs, 40 normed as high and 40 as low in mystery. Each participant is randomly assigned one presentation duration (300 ms, 1 s, 5 s or 10 s, between subjects). In the study phase they memorise 40 photos (20 high, 20 low mystery) shown one at a time for that duration, each followed by a 200 ms fixation dot. In the test phase they see those 40 mixed with the 40 others in random order and answer Old or New for each; after Old they make a remember/know judgment. Age and gender are asked at the end. Rebuilt from Szolosi, Watson & Ruddell (2014), The benefits of mystery in nature on attention: assessing the impacts of presentation duration, Frontiers in Psychology 5: 1360; the images and per-image mystery and fascination norms are from its Data Sheets 1-4 (CC BY 4.0, stored in this template). Analysis as in the paper: per participant and scene type, hit rate = share of studied images answered Old (remember or know) in recog_studied, false-alarm rate = share of new images answered Old in recog_new, corrected recognition = hits minus false alarms; 2 (scene type, within) x 4 (duration, between) mixed ANOVA; remember and know rates per cell as in Table 2. Image ids: 0_N = low mystery, 1_N = high mystery. Differences from the original study: (1) online rather than in the lab; (2) the 40 studied images are drawn at random per participant (20 of each type) instead of the paper's two fixed subsets A and B; (3) the instructions, including the explanation of remember and know, are our wording based on the paper's definitions; (4) the working-memory (Aospan) and dissociative-experience (DES) measures and the separate mystery and fascination rating phases are not included (their per-image norms are stored instead); (5) the gender options are ours.
author: Szolosi, Watson & Ruddell
